Introducing KausaAgent.

Your personal AI research agent that never forgets.

The problem:
Every AI chat starts from zero. You research something today, close the tab, and tomorrow your AI has no idea what you talked about. Weeks of research, gone. Context, lost. You end up repeating yourself over and over.

KausaAgent changes that. Your agent stores every research session into an encrypted knowledge graph. Entities, relationships, decisions, all extracted and indexed automatically. The next time you ask a question, your agent already knows what it learned last week, last month, or three months ago.
The longer you use it, the smarter it gets.

What makes it powerful:
- 86 AI models to choose from (Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, and more)
- Deep research with real-time web search and source analysis
- Knowledge graph that grows with every conversation
- Cross-session memory, your agent carries knowledge forever

What's private:
- Your memory is encrypted with your passphrase. We can't read it. No one can.
- Backed up to IPFS, even if our servers go down, your knowledge is safe
- Wallet-authenticated, no email, no password, just your Solana wallet
- Private inference powered by https://t.co/uBj9NrU0Zs

How to use it:
1. Go to https://t.co/xUDqn7fO0p
2. Connect your Solana wallet
3. Create an agent, set a passphrase
4. Fund with USDC directly from your wallet
5. Start researching. Your agent remembers everything.

In this video, we are doing deep research on neuromorphic computing for autonomous robotics, using KausaAgent with Claude Fable 5.

Built by KausaLayer.

Everyone is obsessed with Claude Fable 5 right now, especially for game development.
Some people even claim that AI agents could replace game developers.
But are we really saying that an AI agent could replace creators like Shigeru Miyamoto, Hideo Kojima, or Hidetaka Miyazaki?

Games are not just code, assets, and mechanics.

Great games are worlds, emotions, stories, and experiences that stay with players for years.
AI will help developers prototype faster, write code, generate ideas, and improve workflows.
But it won’t replace the soul behind great games.

AI is a tool, not the creator.

50 hours with fable 5 and i think a lot of people are using it wrong.

if your task is "write this email", "fix this paragraph", or "answer this question", it's honestly like bringing a bazooka to kill an ant.

you'll get a result, sure. but you're not really using the model.

the biggest lesson for me is that these newer models only start making sense when the task is large enough.

give it a vague objective that requires research, judgment, iteration, tradeoffs, and multiple steps.

something that would take you an hour or two.

that's where it starts to feel different.

the second lesson is that agents reflect who you are.

people talk about prompt engineering. i think we're heading toward manager engineering.

the quality of the outcome is becoming increasingly tied to your ability to describe what you want.

not the exact steps.

the destination.
the taste.
the constraints.

the things you care about.

two people can give the same task to the same model and get wildly different outcomes because one person knows exactly what good looks like and the other doesn't.

that's why i don't think AI is replacing taste.

it's making taste more valuable.

the best results i've gotten from fable 5 weren't from clever prompts.

they came from spending time explaining context, goals, preferences, edge cases, and what success actually looks like.

the model did the execution.

my job was defining the problem properly.

which is starting to feel a lot like managing people.

except the person never sleeps, never gets offended, and can read an entire codebase in a few minutes.

that's the shift i noticed over the last 50 hours.

less time telling the model what to do.

more time figuring out what i actually want.

The headline for me is not the splashy demo. It is that Fable 5 ships with a 319 page system card, explicit bug check caveats, and bio capability notes. The product race is starting to look like governance as a feature.

Fable 5 最反直觉的一点：你给旧模型精心调的 prompt，在它身上是减分项。

最近切模型踩了一圈坑，记几条，都是真实报错换来的：

1. thinking 配置整个删掉。 budget_tokens 会 400，disabled 也 400。它的思考是永远在线的，只能不传或传 adaptive，深度用 effort 控制。temperature 那几个采样参数也全删了。
2. 先查 stop_reason 再读 content。 Fable5 有安全分类器,拒答时返回 200 但 content 是空数组,直接 content[0] 的代码会出问题。加 fallbacks 参数可以让服务端自动落回 Opus 4.8。
3. token 多 30%。 换了分词器，你在 Opus 上算好的成本和 max_tokens 全作废，切之前最好用 count_tokens 拿真实 prompt 重测一遍。
4. 全线 400 先查合规配置。 开了 ZDR 的话，请求写得再对也是 400。我对着请求体查了很久问题根本不在代码里。
5. 单轮能跑十几分钟，超时和流式提前安排好，不然UI看着像是挂了。
6. 回到开头那条：把保姆级 prompt 砍一半。 只留目标和约束，别教它步骤，输出反而更好。

另外就是价格问题，日常的活用 Opus 4.8 就够了。Fable 5 还是留给过夜任务和大重构这种规划类的硬骨头吧。

切之前照这六条核一遍，能省你一下午的 debug。

"I don't prompt Claude anymore. I have loops running that prompt Claude. My job is to write loops." — @bcherny, head of Claude Code at @AnthropicAI 

A loop finds the work, hands it to an agent, checks the result, logs what's done, and decides what's next without you in the middle. You're not prompting anymore. The system is.

Engineers have been building versions of this for years. What's new is that it ships inside the tools now. And the model inside the loop finally got good enough to make it actually work.

That second part is the missing piece. A well-designed loop with a weak model still fails; it makes safe bets instead of structural ones, stores failure notes instead of verified learnings, and rarely consults what it figured out in the last session.

@RLanceMartin tested Claude Fable 5 inside exactly these loops:

→ 6x more pipeline improvements than Opus 4.7 
→ Memory verification coverage jumped from 17% to 73% 
→ Persistent memory improved Fable 5's performance 3x more than Opus 4.8

Stripe compressed months of engineering into a single day, a codebase-wide migration across 50M lines of Ruby that would've taken a whole team over two months by hand.

Anthropic's finding: the longer and more complex the task, the larger Fable 5's lead over every other model.

That's not a coincidence. That's what a model built for loops looks like.

At the highest effort, Fable 5 reflects on and validates its own work, and that's exactly what makes highly autonomous operations possible.

Loop engineering is trending. But it was always the destination. We just didn't have the model that could survive the loop long enough to matter.

Now we do. 👇

I had Claude Fable 5 build a walkable 3D Kyoto neighborhood in Three.js. Runs in the browser.

It's not a single street. There's a connected grid of alleys, intersections, and plazas you can actually wander through. Machiya townhouses, stone lanterns, cherry blossoms, paper lanterns glowing at dusk. A pagoda visible above the rooflines from different streets.

Golden hour and night mode toggle. WASD to walk. Mouse to look around.

Took two prompts. One for the initial build, one to fix the layout so it wasn't a straight corridor. Some areas still feel disconnected and disjointed, but for a browser-rendered 3D neighborhood from two prompts, it's not bad.
